Intensity-Based Estimation of Extreme Value Models for Highly Censored Data via a Latent Poisson Process

Eduardo Janottia,b, Antonio Carlos Pedroso de Limaa, Lígia Henriques-Rodriguesb,c ††thanks: CONTACT Eduardo Janotti. Email: eduardojanotti@ime.usp.br
Abstract

Extreme value theory provides a natural framework for modelling rare events and extrapolating tail probabilities, but its direct application to survival analysis is complicated by right censoring, heterogeneous follow-up, and the need for coherent inference beyond the range of the observed data. We propose a Bayesian survival model that integrates extreme value theory with a hazard-based formulation built upon the extended generalized Pareto distribution. Rather than separating the bulk and tail of the distribution through an explicit threshold, the proposed model represents the entire hazard function within a unified parametric framework, allowing moderate and extreme survival times to be analysed simultaneously while preserving the asymptotic tail behaviour implied by extreme value theory. Inference is performed through a two-stage procedure. First, the hazard function is approximated by a piecewise exponential model. Second, these estimates are linked to the extended generalized Pareto distribution hazard through a hierarchical Bayesian model fitted using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We further develop bias-correction procedures based on latent representative locations and adaptive partition refinement, and establish theoretical results showing the asymptotic consistency of the proposed approximation under standard regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the methodology provides reliable uncertainty quantification across a wide range of tail regimes, censoring proportions, and sample sizes, while remaining robust under moderate model misspecification. The practical performance of the approach is illustrated through an analysis of a heart failure cohort, where the proposed model enables inference on long-term survival probabilities and tail behaviour beyond the observed follow-up period. The resulting framework offers a computationally feasible and theoretically grounded alternative for modelling censored survival data when inference on extreme survival times is of primary scientific interest.

keywords
Bayesian inference; extreme value theory; extended generalized Pareto distribution; hazard modelling; survival analysis

1 Introduction

The statistical modelling of rare and extreme events is fundamental to risk assessment and long-term prediction. Extreme Value Theory (EVT) provides a principled framework for characterizing distributional tails, with the Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) approach and the Generalized Pareto (GP) distribution being among its principal methodologies (5). A central parameter in this framework is the extreme value index (EVI), denoted by ξ\xi, which determines the asymptotic tail behaviour. Positive, zero, and negative values of ξ\xi correspond, respectively, to heavy-tailed distributions with no finite upper endpoint, the Gumbel domain characterized by exponential-type tail decay, and distributions with a finite upper endpoint. Estimation of ξ\xi is therefore essential for characterizing tail behaviour and extrapolating extreme probabilities.

Applying POT-based methods to survival data introduces additional challenges due to right censoring and heterogeneous follow-up times. In particular, information about the extreme survival tail may be limited to a small number of observed events and the censoring pattern, making extrapolation beyond the observed follow-up period difficult. Under substantial censoring, conventional likelihood-based estimation of GP and related tail models can become numerically unstable, with the tail-index estimate ξ\xi being especially sensitive to limited information. These difficulties are particularly relevant when the tail regime is unknown and ξ\xi must be estimated without imposing restrictions associated with a specific domain of attraction.

Several approaches have been developed to address extreme-value estimation under right censoring. Existing methods establish consistency and asymptotic properties for tail-index estimators in the presence of random censoring (37, 8, 9). Related developments include cure-rate models for populations containing individuals who may never experience the event of interest (39, 33), as well as more flexible tail distributions such as the Extended Generalized Pareto (EGP) model, which allows additional flexibility in the body while preserving the asymptotic tail behaviour (31, 29, 38). Despite these developments, stable estimation of GP- and EGP-type models under severe censoring remains challenging, particularly when the tail index is unrestricted.

The present work is motivated by our previous study on extreme survival probabilities under right censoring (23), which introduced a frequentist semi-parametric framework for incorporating extreme-value structure into survival analysis and extrapolating survival probabilities beyond observed follow-up times based on a latent intensity represented by a Log-Gaussian Cox Process (LGCP). That study highlighted computational and inferential difficulties associated with direct likelihood-based estimation in the extreme region. A subsequent work (22) considered a Bayesian extension. While this formulation demonstrated the potential of intensity-based modelling for extreme survival extrapolation, the latent Gaussian-process structure introduces additional modelling and computational complexity, including the numerical treatment of the latent intensity. Related challenges in Gaussian-process maximum likelihood estimation have also been documented in the literature (24, 4).

In this paper, we propose an alternative estimation procedure for GP and EGP tail models based on a latent Poisson-process representation of the intensity associated with the underlying extreme-value model. Unlike the previous LGCP formulation, the proposed approach does not introduce an additional latent Gaussian process, yielding a simpler probabilistic structure and an alternative computational strategy for tail-parameter estimation. The method is designed to address numerical difficulties arising under substantial censoring, with particular emphasis on estimating the tail index ξ\xi without restricting it a priori to a specific tail regime. This allows the data to inform whether the underlying tail is heavy, of Gumbel type, or has a finite upper endpoint.

The proposed framework further provides a basis for extensions to covariate-dependent tail behaviour and bias-correction procedures. These developments are intended to improve the practical use of extreme-value models for long-term survival extrapolation when the available event information is sparse. The methodology is evaluated through simulation studies examining finite-sample performance, numerical stability, and robustness, and is illustrated using a heart failure dataset.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant background on EVT, GP and EGP models, and intensity-based representations for censored survival data. Section 3 introduces the proposed latent Poisson-process formulation and Bayesian estimation procedure. Section 4 develops extensions for covariate-dependent tail behaviour, while Section 5 discusses bias correction based on latent representative locations and adaptive partition refinement. Section 6 presents the simulation studies, and Section 7 provides the heart failure data application. Finally, Section 8 summarizes the findings, limitations, and directions for future research.

2 State of the art and recent developments

2.1 Fundamentals

EVT provides the asymptotic foundations for statistical methods designed to characterize distribution tails and quantify the probability of extreme events. Its main results underpin widely used approaches for modelling extremes, including block maxima and threshold exceedances, and motivate the GP- and EGP-based models considered in this work.

The first cornerstone result is the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem (16, 19), which states that, under suitable conditions and normalization, the maximum of a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables converges in distribution to a non-degenerate limit belonging to the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) family. This theorem establishes the theoretical basis for block-maxima methods and characterizes the possible limiting distributions of normalized maxima.

While block-maxima methods derived from this theorem are theoretically appealing, they can be inefficient in practice because only a subset of the available observations contributes to the analysis. Threshold-based approaches address this limitation through the second fundamental result in EVT, the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem (3, 32). Under suitable regularity conditions, the same as the previous result, this theorem states that the conditional distribution of exceedances above a sufficiently high threshold can be approximated by a GP. Specifically, if FF denotes the cumulative density function (CDF) of a random variable XX with right endpoint xF=sup{x∈ℝ:F⁡(x)<1},x_{F}=\sup\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F(x)<1\}, the conditional excess CDF above a threshold u<xFu<x_{F} is defined by

P⁡(X−u≤y∣X>u)=F⁡(u+y)−F⁡(u)1−F⁡(u),0≤y<xF−u.P(X-u\leq y\mid X>u)=\frac{F(u+y)-F(u)}{1-F(u)},\qquad 0\leq y<x_{F}-u. (1)

For sufficiently large uu, this distribution is well approximated by a GP with scale parameter σ>0\sigma>0 and shape parameter ξ\xi, where ξ\xi is the same EVI as in the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem. Since the GP provides the only possible non-degenerate limiting family for threshold exceedances under the theorem’s conditions, it occupies a central position in POT methodology.

Comprehensive treatments of parametric and semi-parametric inference for GEV and GP models can be found in (14) and (5). While the former emphasizes practical modelling strategies and diagnostic tools, the latter develops a broad range of estimation techniques for tail-related parameters, including semi-parametric approaches.

A persistent challenge in POT modelling is the estimation of the EVI. Likelihood-based inference for the GP can present non-standard behaviour, including parameter-dependent constraints and difficulties near the boundary of the parameter space, while higher-order moments may fail to exist for certain values of ξ\xi. Classical parametric approaches include maximum likelihood and probability-weighted moments (7), while alternative procedures such as the elemental percentile estimator (13) provide direct approaches to tail-index estimation, in some cases under restricted parameter ranges. In semi-parametric settings, moment-based, Pickands, and Hill-type estimators are also widely employed, with their performance depending on the underlying tail behaviour and on the amount of information available in the extreme region (5). These issues become particularly important when the number of extreme observations is small or when the data are subject to substantial censoring. An additional fundamental challenge is the choice of the threshold above which the POT model is fitted, which remains an open problem in extreme value analysis. A threshold that is too low may introduce bias by violating the asymptotic approximation underlying the GP model, whereas a threshold that is too high reduces the number of exceedances available for inference, increasing estimation uncertainty. Consequently, selecting an appropriate threshold requires balancing bias and variance, and this trade-off becomes especially challenging in the presence of limited extreme observations or substantial censoring.

In parallel with EVT, survival analysis focuses on modelling time-to-event data, typically in the presence of censoring. Right-censoring occurs when the event of interest is not observed during the follow-up period, so that the failure time is only known to exceed the censoring time. This mechanism is ubiquitous in medical, reliability, and demographic studies. A particularly important setting is random right-censoring, in which the censoring time follows its own stochastic mechanism and is assumed to be independent of the failure time, possibly conditional on observed covariates. For more details, see (1).

Let XX denote a nonnegative random variable representing the failure time, with density ff and survival function S⁡(x):=P⁡(X>x).S(x):=P(X>x). The hazard function is defined by h⁡(x):=f⁡(x)/S⁡(x),h(x):=f(x)/S(x), whenever S⁡(x)>0S(x)>0.

When censoring is present, the observed time and censoring indicator are

T=min{X,C},Δ=𝕀{X≤C},T=\min\{X,C\},\qquad\Delta=\mathbb{I}\{X\leq C\}, (2)

where CC denotes the censoring time. Under independent censoring, CC is assumed to be independent of XX; more generally, conditional independence may be assumed given observed covariates.

Let (Ti,Δi)i=1n(T_{i},\Delta_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be independent and identically distributed copies of (T,Δ)(T,\Delta), and let (ti,δi)(t_{i},\delta_{i}) denote their observed realizations. The observed follow-up data are therefore (ti,δi)i=1n(t_{i},\delta_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, where

δi={1,if the event is observed at ​ti,0,if the observation is right-censored at ​ti.\delta_{i}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if the event is observed at }t_{i},\\ 0,&\text{if the observation is right-censored at }t_{i}.\end{cases} (3)

Given these observed pairs, the primary inferential target is often the survival function S⁡(x)S(x) or functionals derived from it. Classical nonparametric estimators, such as the Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen estimators, are widely used because of their robustness and relatively weak modelling assumptions (2, 17). However, their ability to provide information about the survival function becomes increasingly limited in the extreme tail. In particular, once the largest observed failure time has been reached, nonparametric estimators do not provide a principled mechanism for extrapolating the survival function to times beyond the observed range. Consequently, estimation of long-term survival probabilities requires additional assumptions or the specification of a parametric or semi-parametric tail model.

These limitations highlight a fundamental disconnect between standard survival-analysis tools and the objectives of extreme-tail inference. Most conventional survival models are not specifically designed to estimate the EVI or to distinguish between heavy-, exponential- and bounded-tail behaviour. Conversely, many classical EVT applications focus on heavy-tailed settings, whereas survival data may exhibit a much broader range of tail behaviours. Biomedical and demographic processes, for example, may be compatible with rapidly decaying tails or with distributions having an effective or finite upper endpoint. Consequently, there is a need for methodological frameworks that integrate EVT principles with survival analysis while allowing the data to inform the relevant tail regime.

This issue is particularly challenging under substantial right-censoring. When few failures are observed in the extreme region, direct likelihood-based estimation of GP parameters may become numerically unstable, and estimation of the EVI can be highly sensitive to the available tail information. In such situations, imposing a priori restrictions on ξ\xi to distinguish between specific tail regimes may facilitate computation but can also constrain the inferential problem. An estimation framework that can accommodate different values of ξ\xi without requiring such regime-specific restrictions is therefore of particular interest for long-term survival extrapolation.

These considerations motivate the developments pursued in this paper. We focus on an alternative intensity-based estimation procedure for GP and EGP models, in which the relevant tail observations are represented through a latent Poisson-process structure. The resulting formulation provides a different computational route to inference on the tail parameters and is designed to improve numerical stability in highly censored settings, with particular emphasis on the estimation of the EVI.

2.2 Some classical alternatives

A substantial work on long-term survival modelling is built around the notion that a non-negligible fraction of the population may never experience the event of interest. (33) provides a thorough review of such models, with particular attention to cure-rate formulations. In this class of models, the population is typically represented as a mixture of susceptible and cured individuals, with the latter characterized by a positive limiting survival probability. The limiting value of the survival function is commonly referred to as the cure fraction, and its estimation plays a central role in long-term survival inference.

From a complementary perspective, several authors have focused on extreme-value inference under right random censoring without explicitly invoking a cure mechanism. In this line of research, the primary objective is the estimation of tail-related quantities, as the EVI and high quantiles, when observations are subject to stochastic censoring. Representative contributions include the incorporation of covariates into GP-based estimators (37), locally robust procedures (15), trimming-based estimators for heavy-tailed data (8), and conditional approaches motivated by economic applications (30). More recently, a general framework for censored extreme-value estimation was developed in (9, 10), extending generalized Hill-type estimators, establishing asymptotic theory, proposing diagnostic and goodness-of-fit tools.

Another classical strategy for retaining information from the entire sample consists of combining separate models for the bulk and the tail of the distribution. In its simplest form, this approach specifies one model below a threshold and a POT-based model above it. In practice, however, a valid hybrid density generally requires appropriate normalization and, when continuity is desired, matching conditions at the threshold. The basic construction can nevertheless be interpreted as a hybrid model in which EVT tools are reserved for the upper tail, while the central part of the data is handled through a conventional survival or regression model. Such formulations are closely related to splicing methods, in which different distributions are combined to represent different regions of the data distribution (25).

Within survival analysis, this idea was explored by Grama et al. (21), who modelled exceedances above a threshold using an exponential distribution, corresponding to a GP with ξ=0\xi=0, while incorporating lower observations through the Kaplan–Meier estimator. Subsequent extensions (20, 40) addressed heterogeneity by combining POT modelling for extremes with Cox-type regression for the bulk of the data, estimated using the Breslow estimator (28) and further refined through penalized likelihood techniques.

While hybrid and slicing-based approaches offer considerable flexibility, they inherit the intrinsic difficulty of threshold selection. The choice of threshold can strongly influence the bias and variance of tail estimates and remains one of the most delicate practical aspects of POT modelling. Numerous data-driven selection rules and alternative threshold-selection procedures have been proposed; a comprehensive overview is given in (6).

Building on this line of research, several authors have developed threshold-free constructions within the EGP framework. In particular, (29) proposed a formulation that preserves GP tail behaviour while allowing the central part of the distribution to vary flexibly through a functional composition involving the GP CDF and a constrained perturbation CDF. This approach avoids explicit threshold selection and exploits the full dataset while maintaining asymptotic tail coherence. Although the original formulation introduced several possible perturbation mechanisms, no formal selection criterion was provided, and the specification remained largely pragmatic.

Subsequent contributions expanded the EGP paradigm. For example, (35, 36, 18, 26) proposed alternative constructions, while (12) incorporated EGP-based structures into distributional regression models. Furthermore, (38) extended the framework to a semi-parametric setting by estimating the perturbation density using Bernstein polynomials rather than fixing it a priori.

Two complementary challenges emerge from the existing literature. On the one hand, censored EVT methods provide principled tools for estimating extreme-value parameters under incomplete observation but may rely on estimators whose numerical behaviour deteriorates when the available tail information is sparse. On the other hand, threshold-free EGP constructions allow the bulk and tail of the distribution to be modelled within a unified framework, but their existing estimation procedures do not directly address the computational difficulties that arise in highly censored settings.

3 The proposed model

We propose a Bayesian survival model that embeds the tail behaviour of the EGP distribution directly into the hazard function. Rather than explicitly separating threshold exceedances from the bulk of the observations, the model specifies the hazard over the entire time domain. The parameters govern the overall hazard shape, while the EVI, ξ\xi, determines its asymptotic tail behaviour. Bayesian inference allows prior information to be incorporated and posterior uncertainty to be quantified.

The model is formulated within a counting-process framework, which provides a natural representation of time-to-event data and connects hazard-based and intensity-based modelling (1). Let Ti=min⁡(Xi,Ci)T_{i}=\min(X_{i},C_{i}) and Δi=𝕀⁡(Xi≤Ci)\Delta_{i}=\mathbb{I}(X_{i}\leq C_{i}) denote the random observed follow-up time and event indicator for individual ii, respectively. For each individual, define the counting process

Ni​(t)=𝕀⁡(Ti≤t,Δi=1),t≥0,N_{i}(t)=\mathbb{I}(T_{i}\leq t,\Delta_{i}=1),\qquad t\geq 0, (4)

which records whether the event has occurred by time tt, and the at-risk process

Yi​(t)=𝕀⁡(Ti≥t),t≥0.Y_{i}(t)=\mathbb{I}(T_{i}\geq t),\qquad t\geq 0. (5)

The counting process has intensity

λi​(t)=Yi​(t)​h​(t),\lambda_{i}(t)=Y_{i}(t)h(t), (6)

where h⁡(t)h(t) is the underlying hazard function. Its Doob–Meyer decomposition is

Ni​(t)=∫0tYi​(u)​h​(u)​𝑑u+Mi​(t),N_{i}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}Y_{i}(u)h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u+M_{i}(t), (7)

where Mi​(t)M_{i}(t) is a local martingale with respect to the underlying filtration.

Building on this representation, we combine extreme value theory with an intensity-based latent Poisson-process formulation to construct an alternative estimation procedure for GP and EGP models. By exploiting information from censored observations, this approach aims to improve the stability of EVI estimation across different tail regimes, while preserving the asymptotic properties implied by the underlying extreme-value model.

3.1 Extended generalized Pareto hazard

Let

G(t;σ,ξ)=1−(1+ξ​tσ)−1/ξ,1+ξ​tσ>0,t>0,G(t;\sigma,\xi)=1-\left(1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi},\qquad 1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}>0,\qquad t>0, (8)

denote the CDF of a GP distribution, where σ>0\sigma>0 is the scale parameter and ξ\xi is the EVI. The corresponding density is

g(t;σ,ξ)=1σ(1+ξ​tσ)−1/ξ−1.g(t;\sigma,\xi)=\frac{1}{\sigma}\left(1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi-1}. (9)

For convenience, define

q(t)=(1+ξ​tσ)−1/ξ.q(t)=\left(1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi}. (10)

Then, G⁡(t,σ,ξ)=1−q⁡(t)G(t;\sigma,\xi)=1-q(t) and g⁡(t,σ,ξ)=1σ​q​(t)1+ξ.g(t;\sigma,\xi)=\frac{1}{\sigma}q(t)^{1+\xi}.

The EGP distribution is obtained by applying a power transformation to the GP CDF, which is defined as

GEGP​(t,σ,ξ,κ)={G⁡(t,σ,ξ)}κ,κ>0,G_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t;\sigma,\xi,\kappa)=\left\{G(t;\sigma,\xi)\right\}^{\kappa},\qquad\kappa>0, (11)

where κ\kappa is an additional shape parameter that controls the departure of the EGP distribution from the standard GP model. In particular, κ=1\kappa=1 recovers the GP distribution, whereas values of κ\kappa different from one modify the distribution of observations away from the asymptotic tail.

Differentiating the EGP CDF with respect to tt gives the corresponding density,

gEGP​(t,σ,ξ,κ)=κ​{G⁡(t,σ,ξ)}κ−1​g​(t,σ,ξ).g_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t;\sigma,\xi,\kappa)=\kappa\left\{G(t;\sigma,\xi)\right\}^{\kappa-1}g(t;\sigma,\xi). (12)

Consequently, the EGP hazard function is

hEGP​(t,σ,ξ,κ)=κ​{G⁡(t,σ,ξ)}κ−1​g​(t,σ,ξ)1−{G⁡(t,σ,ξ)}κ.h_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t;\sigma,\xi,\kappa)=\frac{\kappa\left\{G(t;\sigma,\xi)\right\}^{\kappa-1}g(t;\sigma,\xi)}{1-\left\{G(t;\sigma,\xi)\right\}^{\kappa}}. (13)

Substituting G⁡(t,σ,ξ)=1−q⁡(t)G(t;\sigma,\xi)=1-q(t) and the expression for the GP density yields

hEGP​(t,σ,ξ,κ)=κσ​[1−q⁡(t)]κ−1​q​(t)1+ξ1−[1−q⁡(t)]κ.h_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t;\sigma,\xi,\kappa)=\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}\frac{[1-q(t)]^{\kappa-1}q(t)^{1+\xi}}{1-[1-q(t)]^{\kappa}}. (14)

The parameter κ\kappa determines how the EGP distribution departs from the GP model in the body of the distribution. When 0<κ<10<\kappa<1, the power transformation increases G​(t,σ,ξ)κG(t;\sigma,\xi)^{\kappa} relative to G⁡(t,σ,ξ)G(t;\sigma,\xi), resulting in greater cumulative probability at a given finite value of tt. Conversely, when κ>1\kappa>1, the transformation decreases G​(t,σ,ξ)κG(t;\sigma,\xi)^{\kappa}, resulting in less cumulative probability at the same value of tt. Thus, κ<1\kappa<1 and κ>1\kappa>1 provide two directions of departure from the GP model, while κ=1\kappa=1 corresponds exactly to the standard GP distribution.

Importantly, the power transformation does not alter the first-order tail behaviour determined by the extreme value index ξ\xi. Indeed, as tt approaches the upper tail, G⁡(t,σ,ξ)G(t;\sigma,\xi) approaches one, and the EGP survival function satisfies

1−GEGP​(t,σ,ξ,κ)=1−{G⁡(t,σ,ξ)}κ∼κ⁡[1−G⁡(t,σ,ξ)].1-G_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t;\sigma,\xi,\kappa)=1-\left\{G(t;\sigma,\xi)\right\}^{\kappa}\sim\kappa\left[1-G(t;\sigma,\xi)\right]. (15)

Hence, the EGP distribution retains the same extreme value index ξ\xi as the underlying GP distribution, while κ\kappa provides additional flexibility in modelling the distribution away from the asymptotic tail.

3.2 Two-stage inference

Direct likelihood-based inference for GP models presents difficulties across different tail regimes. In particular, the regularity conditions underlying standard maximum likelihood estimation fail when ξ<−1/2\xi<-1/2, complicating inference for sufficiently negative values of the extreme value index. Conversely, moment-based estimation relies on the existence of the corresponding moments, which imposes restrictions on ξ\xi and limits its applicability for sufficiently heavy-tailed distributions. These difficulties are further aggravated by right censoring, which reduces the information available in the extreme region and makes likelihood evaluation and optimization more challenging. Bayesian procedures provide an alternative, but their computational cost can become substantial for large samples.

To address these limitations, we propose a two-stage approximation that avoids direct evaluation of the likelihood associated with the continuous-time EGP model. Consequently, the procedure does not require a closed-form expression for this likelihood. In the first stage, the censored survival observations are approximated through a piecewise exponential model, yielding interval-specific hazard estimates and their associated uncertainties. This provides a simpler representation of the original data while retaining information about both the estimated hazards and their precision.

In the second stage, these interval-specific estimates are related to the continuous-time EGP model through latent representative locations. The EGP parameters, including the extreme value index ξ\xi, are then estimated from this approximate hazard representation rather than directly from the original censored-data likelihood. This construction separates the estimation of local hazard information from the estimation of the global tail structure, providing an alternative computational strategy for inference under substantial censoring.

The theoretical properties of the proposed construction are established in Appendix A.

Step 1: Piecewise exponential approximation

Let 𝒯=(ρ1,ρM+1]⊂ℝ+\mathcal{T}=(\rho_{1},\rho_{M+1}]\subset\mathbb{R}^{+} denote the time domain over which the hazard function is to be approximated. Consider a sequence of ordered partition points ρ1<ρ2<⋯<ρM+1,\rho_{1}<\rho_{2}<\cdots<\rho_{M+1}, which divides 𝒯\mathcal{T} into MM consecutive intervals, Ij=(ρj,ρj+1]I_{j}=(\rho_{j},\rho_{j+1}], j=1,…,M.j=1,\ldots,M. The hazard function is assumed to be constant within each interval IjI_{j}, yielding the piecewise exponential approximation. The specific procedure used to determine the partition points, including the criterion for dividing the time domain into intervals with similar event patterns, is described in Section 5.2.

Within each interval IjI_{j}, we approximate the hazard by a constant,

h⁡(t)=hj,t∈Ij,h(t)=h_{j},\qquad t\in I_{j}, (16)

with hj>0h_{j}>0. Under this assumption, conditional on being at risk at the beginning of IjI_{j}, the event process within the interval is a homogeneous Poisson process with rate hjh_{j}. Equivalently, by the memoryless property of the exponential distribution, the waiting time from ρj\rho_{j} to an event, conditional on survival to ρj\rho_{j}, is

P⁡(X>ρj+w∣X>ρj)=exp⁡(−hj​w),0≤w≤ρj+1−ρj,P(X>\rho_{j}+w\mid X>\rho_{j})=\exp(-h_{j}w),\qquad 0\leq w\leq\rho_{j+1}-\rho_{j}, (17)

An event occurring within IjI_{j} is therefore observed at its corresponding waiting time, whereas an individual whose observation terminates before an event occurs contributes a right-censored exponential observation at the end of their available follow-up in the interval.

Ei​j:=∫IjYi​(t)​𝑑t=[min⁡(ti,ρj+1)−ρj]+,E_{ij}:=\int_{I_{j}}Y_{i}(t)\,dt=\left[\min(t_{i},\rho_{j+1})-\rho_{j}\right]_{+}, (18)
