Li​j​(hj)=hjDi​j​exp⁡(−hj​Ei​j).L_{ij}(h_{j})=h_{j}^{D_{ij}}\exp\left(-h_{j}E_{ij}\right). (19)

The factor hjDi​jh_{j}^{D_{ij}} accounts for an observed event, while the exponential term accounts for the survival or right-censoring contribution over the corresponding exposure time. Aggregating over individuals, define

Dj\displaystyle D_{j} :=∑i=1nDi​j,\displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{ij}, Ej\displaystyle\qquad E_{j} :=∑i=1nEi​j,\displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}E_{ij}, (20)

where DjD_{j} is the total number of observed events and EjE_{j} is the total exposure time accumulated by all individuals in interval IjI_{j}.

For interval IjI_{j}, the log-likelihood is

ℓj​(hj)=Dj​log⁡(hj)−hj​Ej,\ell_{j}(h_{j})=D_{j}\log(h_{j})-h_{j}E_{j}, (21)

yielding the maximum-likelihood estimate

h^j=DjEj,\widehat{h}_{j}=\frac{D_{j}}{E_{j}}, (22)

and the corresponding estimated standard error

τ^j=ℐj(h^j)−1/2=h^jDj=DjEj,\widehat{\tau}_{j}=\mathcal{I}_{j}(\widehat{h}_{j})^{-1/2}=\frac{\widehat{h}_{j}}{\sqrt{D_{j}}}=\frac{\sqrt{D_{j}}}{E_{j}}, (23)

where ℐj​(h^j)\mathcal{I}_{j}(\widehat{h}_{j}) denotes the observed Fisher information evaluated at the maximum-likelihood estimate. Thus, for each interval with Dj>0D_{j}>0 and Ej>0E_{j}>0, the piecewise exponential approximation is characterized by (h^j,τ^j)(\widehat{h}_{j},\widehat{\tau}_{j}), with estimated hazard function

h^​(t)=∑j=1Mh^j​𝕀​(t∈Ij).\widehat{h}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\widehat{h}_{j}\,\mathbb{I}(t\in I_{j}). (24)

Here, h^j\widehat{h}_{j} estimates the constant hazard assigned to interval IjI_{j}, while τ^j\widehat{\tau}_{j} quantifies the corresponding estimation uncertainty. In particular, the standard error reflects the amount of event information available in each interval, with fewer observed events generally leading to greater estimation uncertainty. This distinction is important when the data are sparse or heavily censored, since the resulting hazard estimates may be less precise.

Intervals with Dj=0D_{j}=0 and Ej>0E_{j}>0 require special consideration. In this case, the likelihood is maximized at the boundary, yielding h^j=0\widehat{h}_{j}=0, rather than a positive interior estimate. However, the observed-information-based standard error is not defined at this boundary estimate. Consequently, such intervals are excluded from the subsequent hazard-location procedure when that procedure requires a positive hazard estimate and a finite standard error.

Because the underlying EGP hazard is generally not constant within IjI_{j}, h^j\widehat{h}_{j} cannot, in general, be associated with a unique deterministic time point. We therefore associate each interval with a latent representative location

Lj∈Ij,ℙ⁡(Lj∈Ij)=1.L_{j}\in I_{j},\qquad\mathbb{P}(L_{j}\in I_{j})=1. (25)

The choice of the latent locations is described in detail in Section 5.3. Figure 1 illustrates the piecewise exponential approximation obtained by partitioning the time domain into intervals Ij=(ρj,ρj+1]I_{j}=(\rho_{j},\rho_{j+1}]. The smooth underlying hazard is approximated within each interval by the constant estimate h^j=Dj/Ej\widehat{h}_{j}=D_{j}/E_{j}, with uncertainty quantified by τ^j=h^j/Dj\widehat{\tau}_{j}=\widehat{h}_{j}/\sqrt{D_{j}}.

Step 2: EGP hazard model

The first step provides, for each interval IjI_{j}, a piecewise exponential hazard estimate h^j\widehat{h}_{j} together with its estimated standard error τ^j\widehat{\tau}_{j}. Since h^j\widehat{h}_{j} summarizes the hazard over an interval rather than at a uniquely defined time point, we use the latent representative location Lj∈IjL_{j}\in I_{j} introduced above to connect the interval-level estimates with the underlying continuous-time EGP hazard.

Conditional on the latent location LjL_{j}, we model the first-stage hazard estimate using the hazard function implied by the EGP model in (14), as follows

h^j|Lj,σ,ξ,κ∼𝒩+​(hEGP​(Lj,σ,ξ,κ),τ^j2),\widehat{h}_{j}\mid L_{j},\sigma,\xi,\kappa\sim\mathcal{N}^{+}\left(h_{\mathrm{EGP}}(L_{j};\sigma,\xi,\kappa),\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}\right), (26)

where 𝒩+​(μ,τ2)\mathcal{N}^{+}(\mu,\tau^{2}) denotes a normal distribution with location parameter μ\mu and scale parameter τ2\tau^{2}, truncated to the positive real line. Note that, due to the truncation, μ\mu and τ2\tau^{2} do not generally coincide with the mean and variance of the resulting distribution. The location parameter is specified by the EGP hazard evaluated at the latent location LjL_{j}, while the scale parameter is determined by the estimated uncertainty from the piecewise exponential approximation. Thus, the second stage does not treat h^j\widehat{h}_{j} as an exact observation of the underlying hazard; instead, it explicitly propagates the estimation uncertainty from Step 1 through τ^j2\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}.

We model the hazard itself, rather than its logarithm, so that the regression remains on the original intensity scale. Positivity is enforced through the truncated normal distribution, which is consistent with the non-negative nature of the hazard.

Combining the two stages, the resulting model can be viewed as a latent-location regression of the piecewise exponential hazard estimates onto the continuous EGP hazard function. The first stage reduces the censored survival data to interval-specific hazard estimates and their associated uncertainties, while the second stage uses the latent locations to map these estimates back to the continuous time scale and estimate the EGP parameters (σ,ξ,κ)(\sigma,\xi,\kappa). The procedure for specifying the latent locations LjL_{j} is given in Section 5.3.

3.3 Prior specification and posterior inference

All model parameters are assumed to be a priori independent. As a weakly informative default specification, the priors for the scale parameter σ\sigma and the EGP shape parameter κ\kappa are

σ∼Lognormal⁡(0,10),κ∼Lognormal⁡(0,10).\sigma\sim\operatorname{Lognormal}(0,10),\qquad\kappa\sim\operatorname{Lognormal}(0,10). (27)

These specifications may be adapted to the application and the available prior information, and are not essential to the parameterization of the extreme value index ξ\xi described below.

The support of the GP distribution imposes a constraint on ξ\xi. Since the model is defined over the time domain 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we require

1+ξ​tσ>0,∀t∈𝒯.1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}>0,\qquad\forall\,t\in\mathcal{T}. (28)

Assuming that 𝒯\mathcal{T} has a finite, positive supremum, this condition is equivalent to

ξ>−σsup𝒯.\xi>-\frac{\sigma}{\sup\mathcal{T}}. (29)

Rather than imposing this constraint directly, we introduce an unconstrained latent parameter with a centered Laplace prior,

ζ∼Laplace⁡(0,1),\zeta\sim\operatorname{Laplace}(0,1), (30)

and define the extreme value index through the transformation

ξ=σsup𝒯​(eζ−1).\xi=\frac{\sigma}{\sup\mathcal{T}}\left(e^{\zeta}-1\right). (31)

For every finite value of ζ\zeta, this transformation guarantees that inequality (29) holds, while allowing ξ\xi to take arbitrarily large positive values. It therefore provides an unconstrained parameterization of the entire admissible range of ξ\xi over the specified time domain.

To characterize the induced prior on ξ\xi, let

a=σsup𝒯,a=\frac{\sigma}{\sup\mathcal{T}}, (32)

so that

ξ=a⁡(eζ−1).\xi=a(e^{\zeta}-1). (33)

Because this transformation is strictly increasing and the Laplace distribution is centered at zero, the median of the induced prior is

median⁡(ξ∣σ)=a⁡(e0−1)=0.\operatorname{median}(\xi\mid\sigma)=a(e^{0}-1)=0. (34)

Thus, the prior is centered at the exponential-tail boundary rather than favouring either a bounded-tail or a heavy-tailed regime a priori.

The induced density follows from a change of variables. Specifically, the inverse transformation and its derivative are

ζ=log⁡(1+ξa),|d​ζd​ξ|=1a+ξ.\zeta=\log\left(1+\frac{\xi}{a}\right),\qquad\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}\zeta}{\mathrm{d}\xi}\right|=\frac{1}{a+\xi}. (35)

Consequently, the conditional density of ξ\xi is

p⁡(ξ∣σ)={12​a,−a<ξ<0,a2​(a+ξ)2,ξ≥0,0,otherwise.p(\xi\mid\sigma)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{2a},&-a<\xi<0,\\[6.0pt] \dfrac{a}{2(a+\xi)^{2}},&\xi\geq 0,\\[6.0pt] 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (36)

The negative component is therefore uniform on the interval (−a,0)(-a,0), conditional on ξ<0\xi<0, and is bounded below by the GP support constraint. The positive component is unbounded and follows a Lomax (Pareto Type II) distribution, allowing for increasingly heavy-tailed behaviour. The resulting prior is asymmetric in both its support and density, despite being centered at zero in the median sense.

The transformation accommodates the three relevant tail regimes:

ξ<0\displaystyle\xi<0 ⟹bounded upper endpoint,\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\text{bounded upper endpoint}, (37)
ξ=0\displaystyle\xi=0 ⟹exponential tail,\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\text{exponential tail},
ξ>0\displaystyle\xi>0 ⟹heavy tail.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\text{heavy tail}.

Moreover, the centered Laplace prior on ζ\zeta assigns equal probability to positive and negative values. Since the transformation is strictly increasing and maps zero to zero, the induced prior satisfies

Pr⁡(ξ<0∣σ)=Pr⁡(ξ>0∣σ)=12.\Pr(\xi<0\mid\sigma)=\Pr(\xi>0\mid\sigma)=\frac{1}{2}. (38)

Hence, the prior allocates equal probability to the bounded-tail and heavy-tailed regimes, while placing their boundary at the exponential-tail case. This balanced allocation in probability holds despite the asymmetric support and shape of the induced density, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Posterior inference is performed using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) (11), as implemented in Stan (34). Let

𝐋=(L1,…,LM)\mathbf{L}=(L_{1},\ldots,L_{M}) (39)

denote the vector of latent representative locations. By incorporating these locations explicitly into the hierarchical model, posterior uncertainty associated with the within-interval evaluation points is propagated to the estimates of σ\sigma, ξ\xi, and κ\kappa. This is particularly important when the partition intervals are sufficiently wide that replacing each interval with a fixed representative point could introduce appreciable discretization bias.

Posterior samples provide estimates of the model parameters and, through the EGP hazard, the corresponding hazard and survival functions, together with their posterior uncertainty. In particular, inference on tail behaviour is obtained directly from the posterior distribution of ξ\xi, allowing uncertainty about the bounded-tail, exponential-tail, and heavy-tailed regimes to be quantified.

4 Model with tail covariates

A key advantage of the proposed framework is its flexibility in allowing covariate effects to act on both the scale of the hazard and the tail behaviour governing extreme survival times. We extend the baseline model by allowing the scale parameter σ\sigma and the extreme value index ξ\xi to depend on covariates. Thus, both the overall time scale of the survival distribution and its asymptotic tail behaviour may vary across individuals with different covariate profiles.

Let 𝒁=(Z1,…,Zp)⊤\boldsymbol{Z}=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{p})^{\top} denote a vector of pp covariates. The scale parameter is modelled using a log-linear specification,

σ⁡(𝒁)=exp⁡(α0+∑k=1qαk​Zk),q≤p,\sigma(\boldsymbol{Z})=\exp\left(\alpha_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{q}\alpha_{k}Z_{k}\right),\qquad q\leq p, (40)

which guarantees a positive scale for every covariate profile. The coefficients α0,…,αq\alpha_{0},\ldots,\alpha_{q} describe the multiplicative effects of the covariates on the overall time scale of the EGP distribution.

The extreme value index is also allowed to depend on the covariates. However, its parameterization must respect the support constraint of the GP distribution. Specifically, the condition

1+ξ⁡(𝒁)σ⁡(𝒁)​t>0,t∈𝒯,1+\frac{\xi(\boldsymbol{Z})}{\sigma(\boldsymbol{Z})}t>0,\qquad t\in\mathcal{T}, (41)

requires

ξ⁡(𝒁)>−σ⁡(𝒁)sup𝒯,\xi(\boldsymbol{Z})>-\frac{\sigma(\boldsymbol{Z})}{\sup\mathcal{T}}, (42)

assuming that 𝒯\mathcal{T} has a finite, positive supremum and contains zero. This constraint must hold for every covariate profile in the relevant covariate space.

To construct a valid parameterization, assume that the covariates are normalized to [0,1][0,1]. Let 𝒞⊆[0,1]p\mathcal{C}\subseteq[0,1]^{p} denote the relevant covariate space and define the common lower-bound parameter

aσ=inf𝒛∈𝒞σ⁡(𝒛)sup𝒯.a_{\sigma}=\inf_{\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{C}}\frac{\sigma(\boldsymbol{z})}{\sup\mathcal{T}}. (43)

Provided that aσ>0a_{\sigma}>0, this bound ensures that satisfying ξ⁡(𝒁)>−aσ\xi(\boldsymbol{Z})>-a_{\sigma} is sufficient to guarantee the support condition in Equation (42) for every covariate profile.

Under the log-linear scale specification in Equation (40), when the first qq covariates range independently over [0,1][0,1], the lower bound can be written as

aσ=1sup𝒯​exp⁡(α0+∑k=1qmin⁡(0,αk)).a_{\sigma}=\frac{1}{\sup\mathcal{T}}\exp\left(\alpha_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{q}\min(0,\alpha_{k})\right). (44)

We introduce a sequential parameterization of the extreme value index using latent variables

ζk​∼ind​Laplace⁡(0,1),k=0,…,p.\zeta_{k}\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Laplace}(0,1),\qquad k=0,\ldots,p. (45)

First, define the initial value

τ0=aσ​(eζ0−1).\tau_{0}=a_{\sigma}\left(e^{\zeta_{0}}-1\right). (46)

This transformation guarantees that τ0>−aσ\tau_{0}>-a_{\sigma} for every finite ζ0\zeta_{0}.

Next, for k=1,…,pk=1,\ldots,p, define the recursive sequence

τk​(𝒁)=τk−1​(𝒁)+{−τk−1​(𝒁)−aσ}​(1−eζk)​Zk,\tau_{k}(\boldsymbol{Z})=\tau_{k-1}(\boldsymbol{Z})+\left\{-\tau_{k-1}(\boldsymbol{Z})-a_{\sigma}\right\}\left(1-e^{\zeta_{k}}\right)Z_{k}, (47)

where τ0​(𝒁)=τ0\tau_{0}(\boldsymbol{Z})=\tau_{0}. Equivalently, the recursion can be expressed as

τk​(𝒁)+aσ={τk−1​(𝒁)+aσ}​{1−Zk+Zk​eζk}.\tau_{k}(\boldsymbol{Z})+a_{\sigma}=\left\{\tau_{k-1}(\boldsymbol{Z})+a_{\sigma}\right\}\left\{1-Z_{k}+Z_{k}e^{\zeta_{k}}\right\}. (48)

Since Zk∈[0,1]Z_{k}\in[0,1] and eζk>0e^{\zeta_{k}}>0, the multiplicative factor in Equation (48) is strictly positive. It follows recursively that

τk(𝒁)>−aσ,k=0,…,p.\tau_{k}(\boldsymbol{Z})>-a_{\sigma},\qquad k=0,\ldots,p. (49)

The final covariate-dependent extreme value index is therefore defined as

ξ​(𝒁)=τp​(𝒁).\xi(\boldsymbol{Z})=\tau_{p}(\boldsymbol{Z}). (50)

By construction,

ξ⁡(𝒁)>−aσ≥−σ⁡(𝒁)sup𝒯,\xi(\boldsymbol{Z})>-a_{\sigma}\geq-\frac{\sigma(\boldsymbol{Z})}{\sup\mathcal{T}}, (51)

so the GP support condition is satisfied throughout the specified covariate space.

This construction allows the extreme value index to take negative, zero, or positive values, corresponding respectively to bounded-tail, exponential-tail, and heavy-tailed behaviour. The sequential parameterization preserves the support constraint without restricting the model to a single tail regime in advance.

Combining the covariate-dependent scale and extreme value index with the latent representative locations introduced in Section 3, the second-stage model becomes

h^j|Lj,𝒁j,𝜶,𝜻,κ∼𝒩+​(hEGP​(Lj,σ⁡(𝒁j),ξ⁡(𝒁j),κ),τ^j2),\widehat{h}_{j}\mid L_{j},\boldsymbol{Z}_{j},\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\zeta},\kappa\sim\mathcal{N}^{+}\left(h_{\mathrm{EGP}}\left(L_{j};\sigma(\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}),\xi(\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}),\kappa\right),\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}\right), (52)

where σ⁡(𝒁j)\sigma(\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}) is given by Equation (40), ξ⁡(𝒁j)\xi(\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}) is defined recursively through Equations (46) and (47), and 𝜻=(ζ0,…,ζp)⊤\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\zeta_{0},\ldots,\zeta_{p})^{\top} denotes the vector of latent variables.

The resulting model allows covariates to affect both the overall scale of survival times and their asymptotic tail behaviour, while accounting for uncertainty in the latent representative locations and propagating first-stage estimation uncertainty through τ^j2\widehat{\tau}_{j}^{2}.

5 Bias correction

The piecewise exponential approximation introduces discretization bias when the underlying hazard varies appreciably within an interval. In the proposed framework, two related mechanisms are of particular relevance. The first arises from representing a continuously varying hazard by a single constant value within each interval. The second is associated with the highly heterogeneous interval widths and exposure times that can arise in heavy-tailed settings, where a small number of extreme observations may strongly influence the final intervals of the partition.

We considered three strategies to mitigate these effects. The first is a best representative approach, in which each interval is represented by a deterministic location chosen so that the hazard at that location matches the average hazard over the interval. This approach was previously implemented in Janotti et al. (22). Although it is theoretically appealing as a correction for within-interval curvature, it did not exhibit the intended behavior in the resulting model and was therefore abandoned. The second strategy is an adaptive partition refinement, in which the interval boundaries are determined using a preliminary estimate of the underlying distribution. This strategy was also considered in Janotti et al. (22) and is retained here, with an important simplification: rather than repeatedly updating the partition as part of an iterative estimation scheme, we use only a first-step approximation based on an initial exponential fit. This avoids the additional computational cost and feedback associated with iterative partition updating. The third strategy, and the main approach considered in this work, is a latent location formulation. Instead of deterministically selecting a single representative point within each interval, the representative location is treated as an unobserved quantity and its uncertainty is incorporated directly into the hierarchical model. Before introducing this formulation, we describe the two sources of bias and the two alternative strategies that motivate it.

5.1 Sources of discretization bias

Consider an interval

Ij=(ℓj,uj),ℓj=infIj,uj=supIj.I_{j}=(\ell_{j},u_{j}),\qquad\ell_{j}=\inf I_{j},\qquad u_{j}=\sup I_{j}. (53)

If the true hazard is h⁡(t)h(t), the expected number of events per unit exposure over the interval is determined by its average hazard,

cj=1uj−ℓj​∫ℓjujh⁡(t)​𝑑t.c_{j}=\frac{1}{u_{j}-\ell_{j}}\int_{\ell_{j}}^{u_{j}}h(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. (54)

For the GP hazard,

h⁡(t)=1σ+ξ​t,1+ξ​tσ>0,h(t)=\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi t},\qquad 1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}>0, (55)

the corresponding average hazard is

cj,ξ=1uj−ℓj​1ξ​log⁡(σ+ξ​ujσ+ξ​ℓj),ξ≠0.c_{j,\xi}=\frac{1}{u_{j}-\ell_{j}}\frac{1}{\xi}\log\left(\frac{\sigma+\xi u_{j}}{\sigma+\xi\ell_{j}}\right),\qquad\xi\neq 0. (56)

For ξ=0\xi=0, the expression is obtained by continuity and reduces to

cj,0=1σ.c_{j,0}=\frac{1}{\sigma}. (57)

The derivation of this expression is provided in Appendix B.

In the piecewise exponential approximation, the continuously varying hazard within IjI_{j} is represented by a single value. A conventional choice is to evaluate the hazard at the midpoint,

mj=ℓj+uj2,m_{j}=\frac{\ell_{j}+u_{j}}{2}, (58)

and use h⁡(mj)h(m_{j}) as the representative hazard. However, the interval-level hazard estimated from the piecewise exponential model corresponds to the average hazard cj,ξc_{j,\xi}, which generally differs from the midpoint value:

h⁡(mj)≠cj,ξ.h(m_{j})\neq c_{j,\xi}. (59)

This discrepancy is a discretization effect arising from the variation of the hazard within the interval. A natural deterministic correction is therefore to select a representative location rj,ξ∈Ijr_{j,\xi}\in I_{j} satisfying

h⁡(rj,ξ)=cj,ξ.h(r_{j,\xi})=c_{j,\xi}. (60)

For the GP hazard, solving this equation gives

rj,ξ=1ξ​(1cj,ξ−σ),ξ≠0.r_{j,\xi}=\frac{1}{\xi}\left(\frac{1}{c_{j,\xi}}-\sigma\right),\qquad\xi\neq 0. (61)

When ξ=0\xi=0, the hazard is constant throughout the interval, so the choice of representative location is immaterial. The midpoint may therefore be used:

rj,0=mj=ℓj+uj2.r_{j,0}=m_{j}=\frac{\ell_{j}+u_{j}}{2}. (62)

The discrepancy between midpoint evaluation and the representative-point construction can be characterized analytically for an interval of width LL beginning at zero, I1=[0,L)I_{1}=[0,L). For the GP hazard, the representative point r1r_{1}, defined by matching the hazard at that point to the interval-average hazard, is

r1=Llog⁡(1+ξ​Lσ)−σξ,m1=L2.r_{1}=\frac{L}{\log\left(1+\frac{\xi L}{\sigma}\right)}-\frac{\sigma}{\xi},\qquad m_{1}=\frac{L}{2}. (63)

Introducing the dimensionless quantity

z=ξ​Lσ,z=\frac{\xi L}{\sigma}, (64)

the relative location of the representative point becomes

R​(z)=r1m1=2​(1log⁡(1+z)−1z).R(z)=\frac{r_{1}}{m_{1}}=2\left(\frac{1}{\log(1+z)}-\frac{1}{z}\right). (65)

As derived in Appendix B, its expansion around zero is

R⁡(z)=1−z6+O⁡(z2),z→0.R(z)=1-\frac{z}{6}+O(z^{2}),\qquad z\to 0. (66)

Thus, the representative point approaches the midpoint as the interval width becomes small relative to the scale of hazard variation. Furthermore, R⁡(z)<1R(z)<1 for z>0z>0 and R⁡(z)>1R(z)>1 for −1<z<0-1<z<0. Consequently, positive values of ξ\xi place the representative point to the left of the midpoint, whereas negative values place it to the right.

This discrepancy may affect the estimation of tail behaviour. Let ξ′\xi^{\prime} denote the index obtained by matching the midpoint hazard to the interval-average hazard. Under the corresponding hazard-matching relationship,

h⁡(r1,σ,ξ)=h⁡(m1,σ,ξ′),h(r_{1};\sigma,\xi)=h(m_{1};\sigma,\xi^{\prime}), (67)

the resulting index is claimed to satisfy

ξ′=ξ​R​(z).\xi^{\prime}=\xi R(z). (68)

Under this relationship, the relative location of the representative point implies

{ξ′<ξ,ξ>0,ξ′>ξ,ξ<0.\begin{cases}\xi^{\prime}<\xi,&\xi>0,\\ \xi^{\prime}>\xi,&\xi<0.\end{cases} (69)

Hence, midpoint representation shifts the matched index towards zero, understating positive tail heaviness and making negative indices less negative. The magnitude of the discrepancy depends on the relative variation of the hazard within the interval, as characterized by |ξ|​L/σ|\xi|L/\sigma.

The representative-point construction addresses this discrepancy at the interval level by defining rjr_{j} such that

h⁡(rj,σ,ξ)=cj,h(r_{j};\sigma,\xi)=c_{j}, (70)

where cjc_{j} denotes the interval-average hazard. This provides a direct correspondence between the continuous GP hazard and the piecewise exponential approximation. However, because rjr_{j} depends deterministically on the unknown parameters (σ,ξ)(\sigma,\xi), incorporating this correction introduces additional dependence into the estimation procedure. Furthermore, its empirical performance was unsatisfactory in the previous implementation. Accordingly, the deterministic representative-point correction was considered but ultimately discarded as a correction mechanism in Janotti et al. (22). The present approach instead modifies the partition and subsequently treats the representative locations probabilistically.

Figure 3 illustrates the discrepancy between midpoint and representative-point evaluation and its dependence on the dimensionless interval width zz. For positive ξ\xi, the decreasing GP hazard places the representative point to the left of the midpoint, with the displacement diminishing as zz approaches zero.

5.1.1 Tail amplification

A second source of instability becomes important in heavy-tailed regimes. For a GP⁡(σ,ξ)\operatorname{GP}(\sigma,\xi) random variable with ξ>0\xi>0, the kkth central moment exists if and only if ξ<1/k.\xi<1/k. This property has direct implications for finite samples. Let X1,…,Xn∼GP⁡(σ,ξ)X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\sim\operatorname{GP}(\sigma,\xi) and denote the associated order statistics by X(1)≤⋯≤X(n).X_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq X_{(n)}. If ξ≥1\xi\geq 1, then 𝔼⁡[X(n)]=∞.\mathbb{E}[X_{(n)}]=\infty. More generally, sufficiently high-order moments of the largest order statistics do not exist. Consequently, extreme observations can have a disproportionate influence on the range of the observed data.

This phenomenon affects the construction of the final intervals in a piecewise exponential representation. If partition boundaries are determined directly from the observed extremes, a small number of very large observations can generate intervals with unusually large widths. The corresponding exposure times can then become very large relative to the number of observed events. As introduced in section 3.2, the piecewise exponential estimator in interval IjI_{j} is h^j=Dj/Ej\widehat{h}_{j}=D_{j}/E_{j}, where DjD_{j} is the number of observed events in the interval and EjE_{j} is the corresponding total exposure time. If the final interval contains only a small number of events but a very large amount of exposure, then h^j\widehat{h}_{j} can become artificially small. Thus, heavy-tailed observations can amplify the discretization effects already present in the piecewise exponential approximation.

The two mechanisms are therefore complementary. Curvature bias results from representing a varying hazard by a single evaluation point, whereas tail amplification results from extreme observations producing highly unequal interval widths and exposure times. The first motivates correcting the representative location, while the second motivates adapting the partition.

5.2 Adaptive partition refinement

A complementary strategy is to modify the partition rather than the representative location. Instead of fixing the interval boundaries independently of the data, they can be chosen according to a preliminary estimate of the underlying distribution. The objective is to distribute the observations more evenly across the intervals and thereby reduce the occurrence of extremely heterogeneous exposure times.

In principle, the partition can be refined using the fitted GP CDF FGP​(⋅,σ^,ξ^)F_{\mathrm{GP}}(\cdot;\widehat{\sigma},\widehat{\xi}). For MM intervals, the boundaries can be chosen approximately according to GP quantiles:

ρj=FGP−1(jM;σ^,ξ^),j=0,…,M,\rho_{j}=F_{\mathrm{GP}}^{-1}\left(\frac{j}{M};\widehat{\sigma},\widehat{\xi}\right),\qquad j=0,\ldots,M, (71)

subject to the relevant truncation and time-domain constraints. This construction assigns approximately equal probability mass to each interval:

FGP(ρj+1;σ^,ξ^)−FGP(ρj;σ^,ξ^)≈1M,j=0,…,M−1.F_{\mathrm{GP}}(\rho_{j+1};\widehat{\sigma},\widehat{\xi})-F_{\mathrm{GP}}(\rho_{j};\widehat{\sigma},\widehat{\xi})\approx\frac{1}{M},\qquad j=0,\ldots,M-1. (72)

An adaptive construction of this type was considered and implemented in Janotti et al. (22).

In the present work, however, we do not use a fully iterative refinement scheme. Instead, we use a first-step approximation in which the event times are initially assumed to follow an exponential distribution, X∼Exp⁡(λ),X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda), with right censoring. The rate parameter is estimated by maximum likelihood from the available censored observations. In particular, if DD denotes the total number of observed events and EE denotes the total exposure time, the maximum likelihood estimator is

λ^0=DE.\widehat{\lambda}_{0}=\frac{D}{E}. (73)

This estimate is then used to construct the partition before fitting the final model. Thus, the partition is determined once, using λ^0\widehat{\lambda}_{0}, and is not updated during estimation of the final model.

The corresponding estimated exponential CDF is

F^0​(t)=1−exp⁡(−λ^0​t),t≥0.\widehat{F}_{0}(t)=1-\exp(-\widehat{\lambda}_{0}t),\qquad t\geq 0. (74)

The associated quantile function is

ρj=F^0−1(jM)=−1λ^0log(1−jM),j=0,…,M−1.\rho_{j}=\widehat{F}_{0}^{-1}\left(\frac{j}{M}\right)=-\frac{1}{\widehat{\lambda}_{0}}\log\left(1-\frac{j}{M}\right),\qquad j=0,\ldots,M-1. (75)

Because the untruncated exponential distribution has an unbounded support, the quantile at j=Mj=M is infinite. In practice, the final boundary must therefore be set by a finite upper time limit, or the quantile construction must be applied to a suitably truncated exponential distribution. The resulting boundaries must also respect the time-domain constraints of the analysis.

This one-step construction provides a simple data-adaptive partition without introducing an additional iterative estimation loop. The partition is determined independently of the parameters estimated by the final model, avoiding the need to repeatedly reconstruct the exposure terms and refit the model as the parameter estimates change. The approach therefore retains the principal benefit of adaptive partitioning while keeping the computational structure of the proposed model fixed.

The adaptive partition addresses primarily the second source of discretization instability, namely the amplification caused by highly unequal interval widths in the presence of extreme observations. It does not, however, explicitly account for uncertainty about the appropriate evaluation point within each interval. This motivates the third strategy, which is the main bias-correction approach adopted in this work.

5.3 Latent location correction

Rather than deterministically replacing the midpoint by a bias-corrected representative, we treat the representative location within each interval as a latent quantity. This allows uncertainty about the appropriate evaluation point to be propagated through the hierarchical model without requiring an iterative correction procedure.

The deterministic representative point introduced above provides the theoretical motivation for this construction. In particular, for the GP hazard, the point rj,ξr_{j,\xi} satisfying h⁡(rj,ξ)=cj,ξh(r_{j,\xi})=c_{j,\xi}, identifies the location at which the continuous hazard coincides with the average hazard represented by the piecewise exponential estimate. However, using rj,ξr_{j,\xi} directly would require its value to be updated as the unknown model parameters change.

Instead, we use a simple probabilistic specification for the latent representative locations. For each interval Ij=(ℓj,uj)I_{j}=(\ell_{j},u_{j}), let

Lj=ℓj+Bj​(uj−ℓj),Bj∼Uniform⁡(0,1).L_{j}=\ell_{j}+B_{j}(u_{j}-\ell_{j}),\qquad B_{j}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1). (76)

Equivalently,

Lj∼Uniform⁡(ℓj,uj).L_{j}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(\ell_{j},u_{j}). (77)

Thus, all locations within an interval are initially assigned equal prior density.

Unlike fixed midpoint evaluation, this specification allows the representative locations to vary within their intervals. The data inform their posterior distributions, and uncertainty in L1,…,LML_{1},\ldots,L_{M} is propagated into inference on (σ,ξ,κ)(\sigma,\xi,\kappa). This provides a flexible alternative to fixing each interval-level hazard estimate h^j\widehat{h}_{j} at the midpoint (ℓj+uj)/2(\ell_{j}+u_{j})/2, although it does not guarantee the elimination of discretization bias.

A more informative alternative would center the location distribution around a deterministic representative point rjr_{j}. For example, the standardized location

Bj=Lj−ℓjuj−ℓjB_{j}=\frac{L_{j}-\ell_{j}}{u_{j}-\ell_{j}} (78)

could follow a beta distribution with parameters chosen to concentrate its mass around the standardized value (rj−ℓj)/(uj−ℓj)(r_{j}-\ell_{j})/(u_{j}-\ell_{j}). Such a specification would allow the degree of concentration around rjr_{j} to be controlled, but would introduce additional modeling choices. We therefore retain the uniform specification as a simple baseline. More elaborate adaptive or iterative approaches to modeling the latent locations are left for future work.

6 Simulation

We conduct two simulation studies to evaluate the finite-sample performance and robustness of the proposed estimation procedure. The first study investigates the effect of the number of bins on posterior uncertainty quantification under correctly specified GP models, while varying the sample size, censoring proportion, and tail behaviour of the censoring distribution. The second study evaluates robustness to model misspecification by generating survival and censoring times from a lognormal distribution.

6.1 Simulation study I: choice of the number of bins

The first simulation study evaluates the effect of the number of bins on the inferential performance of the proposed piecewise exponential approximation. In particular, we investigate whether a relatively small number of bins is sufficient to recover the true GP parameters and provide adequate posterior coverage.

For each simulation replicate ii, let {(Xi,j,Ci,j):j=1,…,n}\left\{(X_{i,j},C_{i,j}):j=1,\ldots,n\right\} denote a sample of independent survival and censoring times. The survival times {Xi,j}j=1n\{X_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{n} are independent and identically distributed, as are the censoring times {Ci,j}j=1n\{C_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{n}, and the two sequences are mutually independent. Specifically, Xi,j∼GP⁡(1,ξ),X_{i,j}\sim\operatorname{GP}(1,\xi), Ci,j∼GP⁡(σc,ξc),C_{i,j}\sim\operatorname{GP}(\sigma^{c},\xi^{c}), where ξ\xi and ξc\xi^{c} are the shape parameters of the survival and censoring distributions, respectively, and σc\sigma^{c} is the scale parameter of the censoring distribution.

The observed follow-up time and censoring indicator are defined as Ti,j=min⁡(Xi,j,Ci,j),T_{i,j}=\min(X_{i,j},C_{i,j}), δi,j=𝟙{Xi,j≤Ci,j}.\delta_{i,j}=\mathds{1}\{X_{i,j}\leq C_{i,j}\}.

Thus, δi,j=1\delta_{i,j}=1 indicates an observed event, whereas δi,j=0\delta_{i,j}=0 indicates right censoring.

We consider the shape parameters ξ∈{−2,0,2},\xi\in\{-2,0,2\}, ξc∈{−2,0,2}.\xi^{c}\in\{-2,0,2\}. The censoring scale parameter σc\sigma^{c} is selected separately for each combination of (ξ,ξc)(\xi,\xi^{c}) to produce approximately 25%25\%, 50%50\%, and 75%75\% censoring. In addition to varying the overall censoring proportion, we vary the tail behaviour of the censoring distribution through ξc\xi^{c}. These two aspects of censoring are not equivalent: two censoring mechanisms can produce similar overall proportions of censored observations while generating very different patterns of censoring over time. The values used in the simulation are reported in Table 1.

The choice of ξc\xi^{c} determines the tail behaviour of the censoring mechanism and therefore the extent to which subjects remain under observation for long periods. When ξc<0\xi^{c}<0, the censoring distribution has a finite upper endpoint, implying that follow-up cannot extend beyond a finite time horizon. This setting is representative of administrative censoring or fixed study-end designs. In particular, when the upper endpoint is common across subjects, it is closely related to the classical Type I (administrative) censoring scheme, in which all individuals are censored at a predetermined study-ending time. More generally, the negative-shape GP allows the censoring times to vary while still imposing a finite maximum follow-up time. If ξc=0\xi^{c}=0, the censoring times follow an exponential distribution and the censoring hazard is constant over time. This provides a memoryless censoring mechanism in which the instantaneous chance of being censored does not depend on the duration of follow-up. Unlike the finite-endpoint case, there is no predetermined maximum censoring time, although long follow-up times become progressively less likely. Lastly, when ξc>0\xi^{c}>0, the censoring distribution is heavy-tailed and has no finite upper endpoint. Consequently, some individuals may remain under observation for very long periods, increasing the probability that extreme survival times are observed rather than censored. This setting represents a more favourable observation regime for tail inference, because the censoring mechanism itself does not impose a finite limit on follow-up and has a heavier tail than the exponential case. These three scenarios therefore represent progressively different follow-up regimes: finite-horizon administrative censoring for ξc<0\xi^{c}<0, memoryless censoring for ξc=0\xi^{c}=0, and heavy-tailed, potentially very long follow-up for ξc>0\xi^{c}>0. Comparing them allows the proposed method to be evaluated under qualitatively distinct censoring mechanisms and, importantly, under different degrees of difficulty in recovering the extreme tail of the survival distribution.

We consider two sample sizes, n∈{100,1000},n\in\{100,1000\}, and, for the proposed model, four possible numbers of bins, M∈{5,10,15,20}.M\in\{5,10,15,20\}. For this simulation study, we fix κ=1,\kappa=1,so that the EGP reduces to the classical GP. This choice isolates the effect of the piecewise exponential approximation and allows the simulation to focus on the estimation of the scale parameter σ\sigma and the extreme value index ξ\xi under different censoring configurations. The effect of estimating κ\kappa is investigated separately in the second simulation study.

Figures 4 and 5 summarize the empirical coverage probabilities of the 90%90\% posterior credible intervals for ξ\xi and σ\sigma, respectively.

The simulation results indicate that a relatively small number of bins provides reliable inferential performance across the scenarios considered. In particular, M=5M=5 and M=10M=10 generally produce empirical coverage probabilities close to the nominal 90%90\% level for both parameters and across the different sample sizes, censoring proportions, and censoring mechanisms. Although coverage tends to become more variable as the number of bins increases, the deterioration is gradual over the range considered.

For the shape parameter ξ\xi (Figure 4), the effect of increasing the number of bins depends on both the sample size and the censoring mechanism. For n=100n=100 under bounded censoring (ξc=−2\xi^{c}=-2), increasing MM generally improves empirical coverage, except in scenarios with relatively low censoring and extreme values of ξ\xi, namely ξ=−2\xi=-2 and ξ=2\xi=2. Under exponential censoring (ξc=0\xi^{c}=0), a similar qualitative pattern is observed, although the improvement is less pronounced. Under heavy-tailed censoring (ξc=2\xi^{c}=2), coverage remains comparatively stable as MM increases, with the main exception being the case ξ=−2\xi=-2 under 25%25\% censoring, where a decrease in coverage is observed.

For n=1000n=1000, the empirical coverage of ξ\xi is generally more stable across the different choices of MM. Under both bounded and exponential censoring, changing the number of bins has a limited effect on coverage, with a slight deterioration for ξ=2\xi=2 and a small improvement for ξ=−2\xi=-2. Under heavy-tailed censoring, the same qualitative pattern persists, although the reduction in coverage for ξ=2\xi=2 becomes more pronounced as the number of bins increases. Overall, increasing MM does not provide a systematic improvement in the coverage of the shape parameter and can introduce additional variability, particularly under strong censoring and extreme values of ξ\xi.

The results for the scale parameter σ\sigma (Figure 5) show a similar qualitative pattern. Increasing the number of bins generally leads to greater variability in empirical coverage, with a tendency toward undercoverage for larger values of MM. The magnitude of this effect varies with the sample size, censoring proportion, and censoring mechanism, but the general pattern is consistent across the simulation scenarios.

The tail behaviour of the censoring distribution has a comparatively smaller effect on coverage than the overall censoring proportion. Similar qualitative patterns are observed under bounded, exponential, and heavy-tailed censoring. This suggests that the proposed procedure is reasonably robust to different censoring tail behaviours. In contrast, the censoring proportion has a more pronounced effect on inferential performance, particularly in the scenarios with heavier censoring.

Overall, the results indicate that the number of bins is an important tuning parameter controlling the trade-off between discretization and statistical variability. Smaller values of MM, particularly M=5M=5 and M=10M=10, provide reliable coverage across most of the scenarios considered, whereas larger values can increase variability and lead to coverage deterioration. Accordingly, we use M=10M=10 as the default specification in the subsequent simulation study. This choice represents a compromise between maintaining sufficient resolution in the piecewise approximation and avoiding excessive variability from using a large number of intervals.

6.2 Simulation study II: robustness to model misspecification

The second simulation study evaluates the robustness of the proposed model under distributional misspecification, that is, when the data-generating distribution does not belong to the EGP family. Specifically, survival times are generated from a lognormal distribution with parameters μ=0\mu=0 and σ=1\sigma=1, and density

f⁡(x,μ,σ)=1x​σ​2​π​exp⁡{−(log⁡x−μ)22​σ2},x>0.f(x;\mu,\sigma)=\frac{1}{x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{(\log x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right\},\qquad x>0. (79)

The censoring times are generated independently from the same lognormal distribution. Because the survival and censoring times are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables, ℙ⁡(X≤C)=ℙ⁡(X>C)=12,\mathbb{P}(X\leq C)=\mathbb{P}(X>C)=\frac{1}{2}, and hence the expected censoring proportion is 50%50\%. As in the first simulation study, the observed follow-up times and censoring indicators are defined by Ti,j=min⁡(Xi,j,Ci,j)T_{i,j}=\min(X_{i,j},C_{i,j}) and δi,j=𝟙{Xi,j≤Ci,j}.\delta_{i,j}=\mathds{1}\{X_{i,j}\leq C_{i,j}\}.

Based on the results of the first simulation study, the number of bins is fixed at M=10.M=10. In contrast to the first study, the parameter κ\kappa is now treated as unknown and is estimated jointly with the remaining model parameters. Following the prior specification in Section 3.3, we assign

κ∼Lognormal⁡(0,10).\kappa\sim\operatorname{Lognormal}(0,10). (80)

For each configuration, 1,0001{,}000 independent simulation replicates are generated. Average posterior summaries of the model parameters are reported in Table 2. In addition, Figure 6 compares the true lognormal density with the densities estimated from the simulation replicates. The individual estimated densities are displayed in grey, the pointwise median estimated density is shown in blue, and the true lognormal density is shown in red. This comparison provides a visual assessment of the ability of the proposed model to approximate the underlying distribution when the EGP assumption is misspecified.

Figure 6 shows that the proposed model can provide a close approximation to the underlying lognormal distribution despite the fact that the data-generating mechanism does not belong to the EGP family. Although the estimated densities exhibit variability across simulation replicates, their overall shapes closely follow the true density. The pointwise median estimated density is particularly close to the true lognormal density, with a small discrepancy around the mode and some redistribution of probability mass toward the lower tail.

This flexibility is partly enabled by the additional parameter κ\kappa, which allows departures from the classical GP shape in the non-extreme part of the distribution while retaining a GP-type tail representation. The corresponding posterior summaries in Table 2 show that the estimated value of κ\kappa increases as the censoring proportion increases, accompanied by increasing posterior variability. The estimated values of ξ\xi are positive across the three censoring levels, indicating that the fitted EGP representation uses a heavy-tailed asymptotic component to approximate the lognormal distribution over the range of the observed data.

It is important to note, however, that the lognormal distribution has extreme value index ξ=0\xi=0 in the asymptotic extreme-value sense. Thus, the positive estimates of ξ\xi should not be interpreted as recovery of the true asymptotic extreme value index. Rather, they reflect the ability of the EGP model to approximate the lognormal tail over the finite, non-asymptotic range represented in the data. Although the lognormal is not regularly varying and therefore does not have a positive asymptotic extreme value index, its tail is heavier than an exponential tail and can exhibit substantial tail heaviness over finite ranges. Consequently, a positive ξ\xi can provide a useful effective approximation to the lognormal tail over the range of survival times accessible in the simulation. The fact that the fitted model does not concentrate around ξ=0\xi=0 is therefore consistent with the distinction between finite-range tail approximation and asymptotic tail behaviour.

These results should consequently be interpreted as an assessment of approximation robustness rather than as evidence that the lognormal distribution belongs to the EGP family. In particular, the positive estimates of ξ\xi illustrate that the fitted EGP representation can use its heavy-tailed component to capture the effective tail behaviour of a lognormal distribution over the observed and extrapolated range, even though its asymptotic extreme value index is zero. Overall, the simulation provides evidence that the proposed intensity-based estimation procedure can retain useful distributional flexibility under moderate model misspecification.

7 Application

To illustrate the proposed methodology, we analyze a real-world dataset consisting of patients diagnosed with heart failure and followed at the Heart Institute of the University of São Paulo Medical School (INCOR–FMUSP), Brazil (27). Heart failure is a complex clinical syndrome in which the heart is unable to pump sufficient blood to meet the body’s metabolic demands and represents a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide.

The original cohort comprised patients who entered the study between July 2003 and March 2014 and were subsequently monitored through regular clinical follow-up. Patients were followed until death or the end of the observation period, with individuals who remained alive or were lost to follow-up treated as right-censored. After data cleaning and consistency checks, the final dataset consisted of 2,982 patients, of whom 1,286 experienced the event of interest (all-cause mortality) and 1,696 (56.87%) were right-censored.

For each patient, the observed survival time was defined as the elapsed time, measured in months, from study entry to either the date of death or the date of the last available follow-up. The analysis uses three variables: follow-up time, the event indicator, and sex. The primary objective is to compare the survival experience of male and female patients using the proposed EGP model. The study population consists of 1,705 male patients (791 deaths and 914 censored observations) and 1,277 female patients (495 deaths and 782 censored observations).

To incorporate the effect of sex, male patients are taken as the reference category. Let Z=0Z=0 denote the male group and Z=1Z=1 the female group. Sex is allowed to affect both the scale and tail parameters, while the EGP parameter κ\kappa is assumed to be common to both groups. This choice reflects the clinical assumption that survival patterns over the very early observation window are broadly similar between males and females, before differences in longer-term survival and tail behaviour become apparent. The shared parameter κ\kappa captures this initial survival pattern, while sex-specific scale and tail parameters allow the groups to differ in their overall survival experience and long-term risk.

σ⁡(Z)=exp⁡(σ0+σ1​Z),ξ⁡(Z)=β0+β1​Z,κ=exp⁡(κ0).\sigma(Z)=\exp(\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}Z),\qquad\xi(Z)=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}Z,\qquad\kappa=\exp(\kappa_{0}). (81)

For a given value of ZZ, define

qZ​(t)={(1+ξ⁡(Z)​tσ⁡(Z))−1/ξ(Z),ξ⁡(Z)≠0,exp⁡{−tσ⁡(Z)},ξ⁡(Z)=0.q_{Z}(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left(1+\frac{\xi(Z)t}{\sigma(Z)}\right)^{-1/\xi(Z)},&\xi(Z)\neq 0,\\[10.0pt] \displaystyle\exp\left\{-\frac{t}{\sigma(Z)}\right\},&\xi(Z)=0.\end{cases} (82)

The EGP hazard is then given by

h⁡(t∣Z)=κσ⁡(Z)​[1−qZ​(t)]κ−1​qZ​(t)1+ξ⁡(Z)1−[1−qZ​(t)]κ.h(t\mid Z)=\frac{\kappa}{\sigma(Z)}\frac{[1-q_{Z}(t)]^{\kappa-1}q_{Z}(t)^{1+\xi(Z)}}{1-[1-q_{Z}(t)]^{\kappa}}. (83)

For the male group (Z=0Z=0), the hazard reduces to

h⁡(t∣Z=0)=h0​(t)=eκ0eσ0​[1−q0​(t)]eκ0−1​q0​(t)1+β01−[1−q0​(t)]eκ0,h(t\mid Z=0)=h_{0}(t)=\frac{e^{\kappa_{0}}}{e^{\sigma_{0}}}\frac{[1-q_{0}(t)]^{e^{\kappa_{0}}-1}q_{0}(t)^{1+\beta_{0}}}{1-[1-q_{0}(t)]^{e^{\kappa_{0}}}}, (84)

where

q0​(t)={(1+β0​teσ0)−1/β0,β0≠0,exp⁡(−teσ0),β0=0.q_{0}(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left(1+\frac{\beta_{0}t}{e^{\sigma_{0}}}\right)^{-1/\beta_{0}},&\beta_{0}\neq 0,\\[8.0pt] \displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{t}{e^{\sigma_{0}}}\right),&\beta_{0}=0.\end{cases} (85)

For the female group (Z=1Z=1), the corresponding hazard is

h⁡(t∣Z=1)=h1​(t)=eκ0eσ0+σ1​[1−q1​(t)]eκ0−1​q1​(t)1+β0+β11−[1−q1​(t)]eκ0,h(t\mid Z=1)=h_{1}(t)=\frac{e^{\kappa_{0}}}{e^{\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}}}\frac{[1-q_{1}(t)]^{e^{\kappa_{0}}-1}q_{1}(t)^{1+\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}}}{1-[1-q_{1}(t)]^{e^{\kappa_{0}}}}, (86)

where

q1​(t)={(1+(β0+β1)​teσ0+σ1)−1/(β0+β1),β0+β1≠0,exp⁡(−teσ0+σ1),β0+β1=0.q_{1}(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left(1+\frac{(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1})t}{e^{\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}}}\right)^{-1/(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1})},&\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}\neq 0,\\[8.0pt] \displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{t}{e^{\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1}}}\right),&\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}=0.\end{cases} (87)

The Bayesian inference procedure and prior distributions follow Sections 3 and 4, respectively, with the additional regression structure for the scale and tail parameters. On the transformed scale, the regression parameters have independent Gaussian priors:

σ0,σ1,κ0∼ind𝒩⁡(0,10).\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1},\kappa_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{ind}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,10). (88)

The coefficients β0\beta_{0} and β1\beta_{1} follow the sequential prior construction described in Section 4, which preserves the admissibility of the GP support over the observed time domain.

Table 3 presents the posterior summaries of the model parameters, while Figure 7 compares the posterior survival curves with the corresponding Kaplan–Meier estimates for male and female patients.

The posterior distributions of the regression coefficients associated with the female group provide different levels of evidence across the model parameters. The 90% credible interval for the tail parameter β1\beta_{1} contains zero, indicating limited evidence that sex affects the extreme value index. Thus, although the estimated posterior median is positive, the data do not provide sufficient evidence of a systematic difference in tail heaviness between male and female patients.

In contrast, the posterior distribution of the scale coefficient σ1\sigma_{1} is entirely positive, with its 90% credible interval excluding zero. This provides evidence of a sex difference in the scale of the survival distribution. Specifically, since the scale is modelled on the logarithmic scale, σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0 implies

σ⁡(1)=exp⁡(σ0+σ1)>exp⁡(σ0)=σ⁡(0).\sigma(1)=\exp(\sigma_{0}+\sigma_{1})>\exp(\sigma_{0})=\sigma(0). (89)

Thus, the results support a difference in the overall survival time scale between females and males, but do not provide equally strong evidence of a sex difference in the asymptotic tail behaviour.

The posterior median survival functions closely follow the corresponding Kaplan–Meier estimates for both sexes, as shown in Figure 7, indicating an adequate fit to the observed data. Although the estimated survival curves remain broadly similar at longer follow-up times, the positive posterior effect on the scale parameter indicates a systematic difference in the time scale of survival between the two groups. At the same time, the absence of strong evidence for β1≠0\beta_{1}\neq 0 suggests that the asymptotic tail behaviour, as characterized by the extreme value index, is not substantially different between male and female patients.

8 Conclusions

This paper introduced a Bayesian framework for long-term survival inference under right censoring based on an intensity representation of the generalized Pareto and extended generalized Pareto distributions. The main contribution is an alternative estimation procedure for GP- and EGP-based survival models that exploits a piecewise exponential representation of the hazard and a latent Poisson-process formulation. This construction avoids the need for direct closed-form likelihood evaluation while retaining the extreme-value structure required for extrapolation beyond the observed follow-up period.

A central advantage of the proposed formulation is that the extreme value index ξ\xi can be estimated without imposing an a priori restriction to a specific tail regime. In particular, the parameterization allows the data to distinguish between finite-endpoint (ξ<0\xi<0), exponential (ξ=0\xi=0), and heavy-tailed (ξ>0\xi>0) behaviour, subject only to the support constraints of the specified time domain. This feature is particularly relevant in survival analysis, where assuming a heavy-tailed distribution in advance may be difficult to justify. The use of the full set of observed follow-up times also avoids the need to select a conventional POT threshold separating bulk and extreme observations.

The proposed two-stage procedure first approximates the continuous hazard by a piecewise exponential model and subsequently treats the resulting interval-specific hazard estimates as noisy observations of the underlying GP or EGP hazard. Latent evaluation locations are introduced to account for the fact that an interval-level hazard estimate does not correspond naturally to a unique deterministic time point. Bayesian inference is then performed using HMC, providing posterior distributions for the scale, tail, and EGP shape parameters and consequently for the extrapolated survival function.

The simulation studies indicate that the proposed procedure provides reliable posterior uncertainty quantification across a broad range of tail regimes, censoring proportions, censoring distributions, and sample sizes. The first simulation study showed that a moderate number of intervals, particularly M=5M=5 or M=10M=10, generally provides satisfactory empirical coverage, with M=10M=10 adopted as the default specification in subsequent experiments. Importantly, the procedure was evaluated for negative, zero, and positive values of ξ\xi, demonstrating that its performance does not depend on imposing a predetermined short- or long-tail assumption. The second simulation study further showed substantial robustness to model misspecification: when the data were generated from a lognormal distribution, the EGP model was able to recover the overall distributional shape despite the data-generating mechanism lying outside the assumed model family.

The application to the heart failure dataset demonstrated how the proposed framework can be used to investigate long-term survival under substantial right censoring. The inclusion of covariate effects on both the scale and tail parameters allows differences between groups to be examined separately in terms of overall survival levels and asymptotic tail behaviour. In the application, the posterior results provided evidence for a difference in the scale parameter between male and female patients, while the posterior credible interval for the tail effect included zero, suggesting limited evidence of a difference in the asymptotic tail behaviour between the two groups.

The bias-correction mechanisms developed in this work provide additional tools for addressing discretization effects arising from the piecewise-exponential approximation. In particular, latent bias-correcting representative locations and adaptive partition refinement can be used to reduce curvature and tail-amplification effects. Nevertheless, they provide a natural direction for improving the procedure in settings where the tail is particularly heavy or where the available sample size is limited.

Several directions for future research remain. A systematic investigation of the adaptive partitioning procedure and its interaction with posterior inference would be particularly valuable, as would principled data-driven selection of the number of intervals and the concentration parameter governing the latent representative locations. Further extensions could consider competing risks, recurrent events, multistate processes, and dependent censoring, thereby broadening the applicability of the proposed intensity-based framework.

Overall, the proposed methodology provides a flexible and computationally tractable alternative for GP and EGP estimation under right censoring. By replacing direct likelihood-based estimation with an intensity-based piecewise Poisson representation, the framework facilitates Bayesian inference for the extreme value index without requiring a priori classification of the tail as short, exponential, or heavy. This combination of extreme-value structure, censoring-aware survival modelling, and Bayesian regularization provides a useful framework for estimating and extrapolating long-term survival probabilities when observations in the extreme tail are sparse or heavily censored.

Appendix A Convergence of the Piecewise Exponential Approximation

This appendix establishes the asymptotic validity of the piecewise exponential approximation used in the proposed two-stage inference procedure. The argument is based on two sources of approximation error: the statistical error associated with estimating the interval-specific hazards and the discretization error arising from replacing the continuous hazard by a piecewise constant function.

Throughout this appendix, we assume that the tail distribution belongs to the generalized Pareto family. This assumption is motivated by the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem, under which the conditional excess distribution above a sufficiently high threshold is asymptotically approximated by a GP. Accordingly, the asymptotic hazard in the tail may be represented by the GP hazard.

Let

T∼GP⁡(σ,ξ),σ>0,T\sim\mathrm{GP}(\sigma,\xi),\qquad\sigma>0,

with hazard function

λ⁡(t)=1σ+ξ​t,\lambda(t)=\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi t},

on its support

1+ξ​tσ>0.1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}>0.

For ξ<0\xi<0, the support has a finite upper endpoint −σ/ξ-\sigma/\xi; for ξ≥0\xi\geq 0, the support is unbounded.

Let 𝒯=[0,T]\mathcal{T}=[0,T] be a fixed compact time interval contained in the support of the distribution, and consider a sequence of partitions

0=ρ1<ρ2<⋯<ρM+1=T,0=\rho_{1}<\rho_{2}<\cdots<\rho_{M+1}=T,

with intervals

Ij=(ρj,ρj+1),j=1,…,M.I_{j}=(\rho_{j},\rho_{j+1}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,M.

Denote the maximal mesh width by

ΔM=max1≤j≤M⁡(ρj+1−ρj).\Delta_{M}=\max_{1\leq j\leq M}(\rho_{j+1}-\rho_{j}).

We consider the asymptotic regime

n→∞,M→∞,ΔM→0,n\to\infty,\qquad M\to\infty,\qquad\Delta_{M}\to 0,

with the number of observed events in each interval increasing with the sample size.

Let N⁡(t)N(t) denote the counting process of observed events and let Y⁡(t)Y(t) denote the corresponding at-risk process. For interval IjI_{j}, define the number of observed events and the total exposure time by

Dj=∫Ijd​N​(t),Ej=∫IjY⁡(t)​𝑑t.D_{j}=\int_{I_{j}}dN(t),\qquad E_{j}=\int_{I_{j}}Y(t)\,dt.

The piecewise exponential estimator of the hazard is

λ^j=DjEj.\widehat{\lambda}_{j}=\frac{D_{j}}{E_{j}}.

Under independent censoring and the usual regularity conditions for counting-process estimators, the compensator of N⁡(t)N(t) is

ΛN​(t)=∫0tY⁡(u)​λ​(u)​𝑑u.\Lambda_{N}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}Y(u)\lambda(u)\,du.

Consequently, the law of large numbers for counting processes implies that, for each fixed interval IjI_{j},

λ^j→𝑝λ¯j,\widehat{\lambda}_{j}\xrightarrow{p}\bar{\lambda}_{j},

where

λ¯j=∫IjY⁡(t)​λ​(t)​𝑑t∫IjY⁡(t)​𝑑t\bar{\lambda}_{j}=\frac{\int_{I_{j}}Y(t)\lambda(t)\,dt}{\int_{I_{j}}Y(t)\,dt}

is the exposure-weighted average hazard over the interval.

The quantity λ¯j\bar{\lambda}_{j} need not equal the hazard at the midpoint of the interval. However, because the GP hazard is continuously differentiable on every compact subset of its support, the discrepancy between the interval average and the hazard evaluated at any point in the interval becomes arbitrarily small as the interval width decreases.

Indeed, for t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T},

λ′​(t)=−ξ(σ+ξ​t)2.\lambda^{\prime}(t)=-\frac{\xi}{(\sigma+\xi t)^{2}}.

Since 𝒯\mathcal{T} is compact and lies in the interior of the support, there exists a finite constant CT>0C_{T}>0 such that

supt∈𝒯|λ′​(t)|≤CT.\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}|\lambda^{\prime}(t)|\leq C_{T}.

Therefore, for any s,t∈Ijs,t\in I_{j},

|λ⁡(s)−λ⁡(t)|≤CT​|s−t|≤CT​ΔM.|\lambda(s)-\lambda(t)|\leq C_{T}|s-t|\leq C_{T}\Delta_{M}.

Since λ¯j\bar{\lambda}_{j} is a weighted average of λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) over IjI_{j}, it follows that, for any tj∈Ijt_{j}\in I_{j},

|λ¯j−λ⁡(tj)|≤CT​ΔM.|\bar{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(t_{j})|\leq C_{T}\Delta_{M}.

Hence,

max1≤j≤M⁡|λ¯j−λ⁡(tj)|≤CT​ΔM⟶0.\max_{1\leq j\leq M}|\bar{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(t_{j})|\leq C_{T}\Delta_{M}\longrightarrow 0.

Thus, the discretization error vanishes as the maximum interval width tends to zero. Combining this result with the consistency of the interval hazard estimators yields

λ^j−λ⁡(tj)=(λ^j−λ¯j)+(λ¯j−λ⁡(tj))→𝑝0,\widehat{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(t_{j})=\left(\widehat{\lambda}_{j}-\bar{\lambda}_{j}\right)+\left(\bar{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(t_{j})\right)\xrightarrow{p}0,

provided that the number of events and the corresponding exposure in each interval are sufficiently large.

Proposition A.1 (Consistency of the piecewise exponential approximation).

Assume that the true hazard is the hazard of a GP on a compact interval 𝒯=[0,T]\mathcal{T}=[0,T] contained in the interior of its support. Suppose that censoring is independent and that the counting-process regularity conditions required for consistency of the Nelson–Aalen type interval hazard estimator hold. Let the partition satisfy

ΔM→0\Delta_{M}\to 0

and suppose that the number of observed events and the exposure time in each interval increase sufficiently rapidly with nn. Then, for any sequence of representative points tj∈Ijt_{j}\in I_{j},

max1≤j≤M⁡|λ^j−λ⁡(tj)|→𝑝0.\max_{1\leq j\leq M}\left|\widehat{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(t_{j})\right|\xrightarrow{p}0.
Proof.

The interval estimator converges to the exposure-weighted average hazard,

λ^j−λ¯j→𝑝0.\widehat{\lambda}_{j}-\bar{\lambda}_{j}\xrightarrow{p}0.

Moreover, the differentiability of the GP hazard on the compact interval implies

maxj⁡|λ¯j−λ⁡(tj)|≤CT​ΔM⟶0.\max_{j}|\bar{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(t_{j})|\leq C_{T}\Delta_{M}\longrightarrow 0.

The result follows from the triangle inequality. ∎

The latent evaluation locations introduced in the main text can therefore be interpreted as a probabilistic representation of the fact that an interval-specific hazard estimate corresponds to an interval rather than to a unique deterministic time point. In particular, if

Lj∈Ij,L_{j}\in I_{j},

then the Lipschitz property of the hazard gives

|λ⁡(Lj)−λ⁡(tj)|≤CT​ΔM.|\lambda(L_{j})-\lambda(t_{j})|\leq C_{T}\Delta_{M}.

Consequently,

maxj⁡|λ⁡(Lj)−λ⁡(tj)|→0.\max_{j}|\lambda(L_{j})-\lambda(t_{j})|\xrightarrow{}0.

Combining this result with Proposition A.1 gives

maxj⁡|λ^j−λ⁡(Lj)|→𝑝0.\max_{j}|\widehat{\lambda}_{j}-\lambda(L_{j})|\xrightarrow{p}0.

Importantly, this result does not require LjL_{j} to be uniformly distributed. The asymptotic argument only requires Lj∈IjL_{j}\in I_{j}. The uniform distribution adopted in the main model is a modelling choice used to represent uncertainty about the location of the interval-specific hazard and is not required for consistency.

A.1 Extension to the EGP hazard

The same argument applies to the EGP hazard provided that its parameters remain in the interior of the admissible parameter space and the resulting hazard is continuously differentiable on the compact time interval under consideration.

Recall that the EGP hazard is

hEGP​(t,σ,ξ,κ)=κσ​[1−q⁡(t)]κ−1​q​(t)1+ξ1−[1−q⁡(t)]κ,h_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t;\sigma,\xi,\kappa)=\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}\frac{[1-q(t)]^{\kappa-1}q(t)^{1+\xi}}{1-[1-q(t)]^{\kappa}},

where

q(t)=(1+ξ​tσ)−1/ξ.q(t)=\left(1+\frac{\xi t}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi}.

For any compact interval contained in the interior of the support and for admissible parameter values, hEGPh_{\mathrm{EGP}} is continuous and continuously differentiable. Therefore, the same Lipschitz argument yields

maxj⁡|h¯j−hEGP​(tj,σ,ξ,κ)|≤C​ΔM⟶0,\max_{j}\left|\bar{h}_{j}-h_{\mathrm{EGP}}(t_{j};\sigma,\xi,\kappa)\right|\leq C\Delta_{M}\longrightarrow 0,

for some finite constant CC.

Hence, the piecewise exponential approximation is asymptotically valid for both the classical GP hazard and its EGP extension.

A.2 Remarks on the infinite horizon

The preceding results are established on compact subsets of the support. This restriction is important and should not be interpreted as implying uniform convergence of the hazard on the entire half-line.

For ξ≥0\xi\geq 0, the GP support is unbounded, but the hazard may become arbitrarily small as tt increases. For ξ<0\xi<0, the distribution has a finite upper endpoint

tF=−σξ,t_{F}=-\frac{\sigma}{\xi},

and the hazard diverges as tt approaches this endpoint. Consequently, uniform approximation over the entire support cannot in general be obtained from the compact-interval argument alone.

For any fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, however, one may restrict attention to a compact interval

𝒯ε=[0,ρε]\mathcal{T}_{\varepsilon}=[0,\rho_{\varepsilon}]

contained in the interior of the support. The preceding results then imply that

supt∈𝒯ε|λ^M​(t)−λ⁡(t)|→𝑝0\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\varepsilon}}|\widehat{\lambda}_{M}(t)-\lambda(t)|\xrightarrow{p}0

as the sample size increases and the maximum partition width decreases.

For ξ≥0\xi\geq 0, because the GP survival function satisfies

S⁡(t)→0as ​t→∞,S(t)\to 0\qquad\text{as }t\to\infty,

ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} can additionally be chosen so that

S⁡(ρε)<ε.S(\rho_{\varepsilon})<\varepsilon.

Thus, the probability of observing an event beyond ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} is smaller than ε\varepsilon. This provides a probabilistic justification for restricting the approximation to a sufficiently large finite time horizon when the objective is survival inference over the observationally relevant region.

For ξ<0\xi<0, the corresponding restriction is naturally imposed below the finite endpoint tFt_{F}. In this case, compact subsets bounded away from tFt_{F} are required for the uniform convergence argument.

Proposition A.2 (Compact-set convergence).

Under the assumptions of Proposition A.1, let 𝒦\mathcal{K} be any compact subset of the interior of the GP or EGP support. Then the piecewise exponential approximation converges uniformly in probability to the corresponding true hazard on 𝒦\mathcal{K}:

supt∈𝒦|λ^M​(t)−λ⁡(t)|→𝑝0.\sup_{t\in\mathcal{K}}\left|\widehat{\lambda}_{M}(t)-\lambda(t)\right|\xrightarrow{p}0.

Therefore, the proposed two-stage procedure is asymptotically coherent on every compact subset of the admissible time domain. The approximation error has two components: statistical estimation error, which vanishes as the sample size and interval exposure increase, and discretization error, which vanishes as the maximum partition width tends to zero. This provides the theoretical justification for using the piecewise exponential representation as an approximation to the continuous GP or EGP hazard in the proposed Bayesian inference procedure.

Appendix B Convergence analysis of the bias correction procedure

This appendix studies the effect of interval discretization on the estimation of the extreme value index and provides theoretical justification for the proposed representative-point correction. For simplicity, the analysis is conducted for the standard GP, whose hazard function is

h⁡(x)=1σ+ξ​x.h(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi x}.

The case ξ=0\xi=0 corresponds to the exponential distribution, for which the hazard is constant and discretization therefore introduces no bias. We henceforth restrict attention to ξ≠0\xi\neq 0.

The analysis relies on the stability of the GP under threshold exceedances. In particular, let τ\tau be a threshold satisfying

1+ξ​τσ>0.1+\frac{\xi\tau}{\sigma}>0.

Using the GP survival function,

F¯(x)=ℙ(X>x)=(1+ξ​xσ)−1/ξ,\overline{F}(x)=\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\left(1+\frac{\xi x}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi},

the survival function of the excess variable

Y=X−τ|X>τY=X-\tau\mid X>\tau

is

ℙ⁡(Y>y)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(Y>y) =ℙ⁡(X>τ+y∣X>τ)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(X>\tau+y\mid X>\tau)
=F¯​(τ+y)F¯​(τ)\displaystyle=\frac{\overline{F}(\tau+y)}{\overline{F}(\tau)}
=[1+ξ⁡(τ+y)σ1+ξ​τσ]−1/ξ\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1+\frac{\xi(\tau+y)}{\sigma}}{1+\frac{\xi\tau}{\sigma}}\right]^{-1/\xi}
=(1+ξ​yσ+ξ​τ)−1/ξ.\displaystyle=\left(1+\frac{\xi y}{\sigma+\xi\tau}\right)^{-1/\xi}.

Therefore,

X−τ|X>τ∼GP⁡(σ+ξ​τ,ξ).X-\tau\mid X>\tau\sim\operatorname{GP}(\sigma+\xi\tau,\xi).

Thus, thresholding changes only the scale parameter, from σ\sigma to

στ=σ+ξ​τ,\sigma_{\tau}=\sigma+\xi\tau,

while preserving the extreme value index ξ\xi. This result allows the discretization analysis to be transferred from an interval beginning at zero to any subsequent interval. Specifically, conditional on exceeding the lower endpoint ℓj\ell_{j} of an interval, the excess time

X−ℓj|X>ℓjX-\ell_{j}\mid X>\ell_{j}

follows a GP with scale

σj=σ+ξ​ℓj\sigma_{j}=\sigma+\xi\ell_{j}

and the same shape parameter ξ\xi. Consequently, the representative-point analysis can be carried out without loss of generality on a first interval of the form

I1=[0,L),I_{1}=[0,L),

with the results for subsequent intervals obtained by replacing σ\sigma with the corresponding threshold-adjusted scale σj\sigma_{j}.

B.1 Representative point associated with the interval-average hazard

Consider the interval

I1=[0,L).I_{1}=[0,L).

The average hazard over this interval is

h¯=1L​∫0L1σ+ξ​t​𝑑t.\bar{h}=\frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L}\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi t}\,dt.

Evaluating the integral yields

h¯=1ξ​L​log⁡(1+ξ​Lσ).\bar{h}=\frac{1}{\xi L}\log\left(1+\frac{\xi L}{\sigma}\right).

Define the representative point r1r_{1} as the location satisfying

h⁡(r1)=h¯.h(r_{1})=\bar{h}.

Substituting the GP hazard gives

1σ+ξ​r1=1ξ​L​log⁡(1+ξ​Lσ).\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi r_{1}}=\frac{1}{\xi L}\log\left(1+\frac{\xi L}{\sigma}\right).

Solving for r1r_{1} yields

r1=Llog⁡(1+ξ​Lσ)−σξ.r_{1}=\frac{L}{\log\!\left(1+\frac{\xi L}{\sigma}\right)}-\frac{\sigma}{\xi}.

The conventional midpoint approximation instead evaluates the hazard at

x1=L2.x_{1}=\frac{L}{2}.

The discrepancy between these two evaluation points determines the discretization bias.

B.2 Comparison with midpoint evaluation

Introduce the ratio

R⁡(L,σ,ξ)=r1x1.R(L,\sigma,\xi)=\frac{r_{1}}{x_{1}}.

Substituting the expressions above gives

R⁡(L,σ,ξ)=2​(1log⁡(1+ξ​Lσ)−σξ​L).R(L,\sigma,\xi)=2\left(\frac{1}{\log\!\left(1+\frac{\xi L}{\sigma}\right)}-\frac{\sigma}{\xi L}\right).

Since the ratio depends only on the dimensionless quantity

z=ξ​Lσ,z=\frac{\xi L}{\sigma},

we may write

R​(z)=2​(1log⁡(1+z)−1z).R(z)=2\left(\frac{1}{\log(1+z)}-\frac{1}{z}\right).

Using the expansion

log⁡(1+z)=z−z22+O⁡(z3),\log(1+z)=z-\frac{z^{2}}{2}+O(z^{3}),

it follows that

R⁡(z)=1−z6+O⁡(z2).R(z)=1-\frac{z}{6}+O(z^{2}).

Therefore,

limz→0R⁡(z)=1,\lim_{z\to 0}R(z)=1,

showing that the midpoint and representative point coincide asymptotically as the interval width tends to zero.

Differentiating gives

R′​(z)=2​(1z2−1(1+z)​log2⁡(1+z)).R^{\prime}(z)=2\left(\frac{1}{z^{2}}-\frac{1}{(1+z)\log^{2}(1+z)}\right).

For z>0z>0,

R′​(z)<0,R^{\prime}(z)<0,

and therefore R⁡(z)R(z) is strictly decreasing. Since R⁡(0)=1R(0)=1, we obtain

R⁡(z)<1,z>0,R(z)<1,\qquad z>0,

and

R⁡(z)>1,z<0.R(z)>1,\qquad z<0.

Consequently,

ξ>0⟹r1<x1,\xi>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{1}<x_{1},

while

ξ<0⟹r1>x1.\xi<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{1}>x_{1}.

The discrepancy increases as |ξ|​L/σ|\xi|L/\sigma grows.

B.3 Attenuation of the extreme value index

Suppose that the interval-average hazard is replaced by midpoint evaluation. Let ξ′\xi^{\prime} denote the parameter obtained by matching

h⁡(r1,σ,ξ)=h⁡(x1,σ,ξ′).h(r_{1};\sigma,\xi)=h(x_{1};\sigma,\xi^{\prime}).

Using the GP hazard,

1σ+ξ​r1=1σ+ξ′​x1.\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi r_{1}}=\frac{1}{\sigma+\xi^{\prime}x_{1}}.

Therefore,

ξ′=ξ​r1x1=ξ​R​(L,σ,ξ).\xi^{\prime}=\xi\frac{r_{1}}{x_{1}}=\xi R(L,\sigma,\xi).

From the behaviour of R⁡(z)R(z), it follows that

ξ′<ξ,ξ≠0.\xi^{\prime}<\xi,\qquad\xi\neq 0.

Thus, midpoint evaluation systematically underestimates the extreme value index, resulting in a shorter estimated tail. This bias arises because the midpoint x1=L/2x_{1}=L/2 does not coincide with the representative point associated with the interval-average hazard. As a consequence, replacing the average hazard within an interval by its value at the midpoint leads to a distorted characterization of the tail behaviour.

The proposed correction instead evaluates the hazard at a representative point r⁡(ξ)r(\xi) satisfying

h⁡(r⁡(ξ))=1L​∫0Lh⁡(t)​𝑑t.h(r(\xi))=\frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L}h(t)\,dt.

By construction, the hazard evaluated at r⁡(ξ)r(\xi) coincides exactly with the interval-average hazard. The discrepancy introduced by midpoint evaluation is therefore removed, yielding a representative point that correctly reflects the average behaviour of the hazard within the interval.

In summary, midpoint discretization introduces a systematic negative bias in the estimated extreme value index. For heavy-tailed distributions (ξ>0\xi>0), this results in underestimation of tail heaviness and consequently shorter estimated tails. The proposed representative-point correction eliminates this source of bias by aligning the evaluation location with the interval-average hazard, thereby providing a more faithful approximation of the underlying hazard structure.
